title: Token Entropy Costing Playbook
content:
Context and goal:
- Quick personal playbook for a new pricing knob: 'token entropy' as a supplement to raw token counts.
- Purpose: capture extra value when requests are more 'information-dense' or computationally expensive (long context, high numeric/structured content, high sampling).
- Use as an experimental additive charge that nudges heavy/expensive usage without penalizing typical chat traffic.

Key intuition:
- Not all tokens are equal: some requests cost more GPU cycles (wide attention, long KV lifetimes, high top-k sampling, retrieval passes).
- Define a cheap heuristic metric that correlates with backend cost and/or SLA pressure: token_entropy_score (TES) in [0,1].
- Price = base_per_token * tokens + alpha * TES * tokens (or alpha * TES) depending on design.

Candidate inputs to TES (cheap / computable at API layer):
1) avg_input_token_length (long tokens => lower entropy, but long context increases KV lifecycle)
2) context_window_fraction = requested_context / model_max_context
3) sampling_intensity = temperature>0.8 or top_p>0.9 -> raises cost flag
4) multi_step_tools = presence of tool calls / function serial calls (binary boost)
5) embed+search_count = number of retrieval vectors requested pre-gen
6) prompt_complexity_hint = special markers from SDK (customer-supplied complexity label)

Simple scoring sketch (cheap):
- norm_context = min(1.0, context_window_fraction * 1.2)
- sampling_factor = (temperature>0.8 or top_p>0.95) ? 1.0 : 0.0
- tool_flag = has_tool_calls ? 1.0 : 0.0
- retrieval_frac = min(1.0, embed+search_count / 5)
- TES = clamp(0, 1, 0.4*norm_context + 0.2*sampling_factor + 0.2*tool_flag + 0.2*retrieval_frac)

Pricing variants (back-of-envelope):
A) Per-token additive: price = base * tokens + alpha * TES * tokens - base = $0.00001 / token (example low-end) - alpha = $0.00002 (so at TES=1, additional $0.00002/token)
B) Per-call surcharge: price = base * tokens + beta * TES - beta = $0.005 per high-entropy call (captures small numbers of tokens with heavy sidecosts)
C) Hybrid: small per-token alpha plus small per-call beta to capture both scale and tail costs.

Micro-Econ anchors and calibrations (rough):
Assumptions (hosted GPU efficient runtime):
- amortized GPU cost per active token generation (including KV memory pressure and batching) = $0.000006/token (measured from recent logs on mixed load) - infra overhead + control plane + margins = ~1.8x -> target cost recovery per token baseline = $0.000011/token
- worst-case high-entropy sessions (long context + retrieval + tools) impose ~4x more infra work (cache churn, more traces, small batches).

Scenario math (100k tokens/month heavy cohort):
- baseline only pricing (no entropy): revenue = 100k * $0.000011 = $1.10
- with TES additive (alpha $0.00002) and average TES=0.6: extra = 100k * 0.00002 * 0.6 = $1.20 -> total $2.30
- This recovers ~2.1x of baseline cost for heavy cohort vs baseline recovery 1x.

Design tradeoffs and product shaping:
- Transparency: user-facing TES label + brief reason ("long context surcharge") to avoid surprise. Offer TES diagnostic headers in response.
- Opt-in vs default: start as opt-in experiment (billing preview) for a subset of customers.
- SDK flags: let customers annotate 'expected_complexity' so they can declare high complexity and accept surcharges or get discounted committed rates.
- Protect small users: floor-free tokens per day (e.g., first 1k tokens in a call ignored for TES).

Tier ideas incorporating TES (experimental):
- Hobby: flat per-token, TES ignored (simple). Good for adoption.
- Professional: per-token billing + TES additive, small monthly commit, 5% discount if precommit.
- Team/Platform: pooled tokens with TES applied to per-call surcharges, optional negotiated cap on TES-exposure.
- Enterprise: dedicated routing to capacity (TES disabled as a surcharge if on Dedicated — handled via separate capacity pricing).

Implementation notes (cheap, low-friction):
- Compute TES in API gateway layer (stateless heuristics) and return X-TES header.
- Ship a logging flag to collect correlation between TES and actual GPU cycle accounting (trace ids). Use this for calibration over 4–8 weeks.
- Backstop: cap TES surcharge per-call to avoid billing shock (e.g., $2 max per call).

Experiment plan (6 weeks):
Week 0: implement TES calc + header + internal dashboard.
Weeks 1–2: collect baseline mapping TES -> measured GPU cycles across 50k calls.
Weeks 3–4: trial alpha additive on opt-in cohort (5% of paying users) as billing-preview only.
Weeks 5–6: enable soft charges for cohort (invoice notes) and monitor churn/feedback.

Open questions / risks:
- Can TES be gamed? (customers split requests into multiple calls to avoid high TES) -> need per-session smoothing or per-account rolling window.
- Regulatory/contract risk: enterprise customers may object to opaque surcharges. Require clear notice and opt-out path.
- Measurement drift: kernel improvements in runtime could change correlation; maintain weekly recalibration.

Notes to self:
- Hook to existing amortized-gpu-hour-to-token backcalc doc and compare numbers.
- Keep alpha small initially; aim to test signal, not monetize aggressively.
- Simple UI: show last-call TES in console with a short hint and 'why this call was charged' link.

Quick scratch calcs (examples):
- 2k token call with TES=0.8, variant A: base 0.000011*2000 = $0.022, alpha=0.00002*2000*0.8=$0.032 -> total $0.054
- Same call variant B (beta=0.005): base $0.022 + 0.005*0.8=$0.004 -> total $0.026
- Observations: additive-per-token makes high-token heavy calls scale cost linearly; per-call beta better for many short but complex calls.

Next steps:
- Draft a short customer-facing note for SDK preview and a simple console tooltip.
- Ask SRE/infra for quick run to map TES->p99 cpu/gpu cycles for a week.
- Prepare billing preview dataset and a simple AB test design (treatment=pricing preview header + explanatory note).

End of notebook.

(MT — personal scratchpad; not approved product policy)
